scenes.tts: Why does fast population growth bend instead of climbing forever? Watch a Chesapeake creek as the blue crab population changes. The water keeps moving, but food and hiding places are limited. Predators and disease also affect survival. Something in this picture must push back as the population grows.

scenes.visual: Hook on a full-frame cross-section of one schematic Chesapeake creek. Teal crab cartoons drift over a sandy bottom; gold food dots circulate; green grass blades sway; red predator and disease arrows wait at the edges. A small population tracker rises as new crabs appear. Put the question high in the frame, then transform it into a compact corner label. Mark the entire world 'schematic'.

scenes.visual: Keep the moving creek dimly visible. Brief title card: Why Growth Bends. Preserve the teal population, gold food, green shelter, red living-challenge and pale-blue cold-water colour map for every later scene.

scenes.tts: A population is all the members of one species living in the same area at the same time. Teal crab symbols track its size. Gold food and green shelter show resources. Red arrows show living challenges, such as predators and disease. A pale blue band shows cold water, a nonliving challenge. Together, these living and nonliving factors can limit growth.

scenes.visual: Return the creek to full brightness. Gather teal crabs inside a boundary labelled 'population'. As each factor is named, move its existing object toward the boundary, including a pale blue cold-water band at the creek edge for the nonliving challenge, instead of adding label chips. A slim legend grows from the five existing colours: teal population, gold food, green shelter, red living challenges and pale-blue cold water. Keep no more than the population, food, shelter, predator, disease, cold-water band and legend visible.

scenes.tts: Start with a small population and plentiful resources. The population increases by the same fraction each step, so the number added grows. That pattern is exponential growth. Its computed curve bends upward like a jay. This model is schematic, but the curve follows its stated rule.
scenes.caption: Start with a small population and plentiful resources. The population increases by the same fraction each step, so the number added grows. That pattern is exponential growth. Its computed curve bends upward like a J. This model is schematic, but the curve follows its stated rule.
scenes.visual: Keep the creek on the left and grow a graph from its right edge. Compute points from a stated made-up exponential rule and label the axes 'time' and 'population size'. Show any values only on screen. With each computed point, add matching teal crabs while gold food remains abundant. Label the plot 'computed model'.
scenes.narration: Start with a small population and plentiful resources. The population increases by the same fraction each step, so the number added grows. That pattern is exponential growth. Its computed curve bends upward like a J. This model is schematic, but the curve follows its stated rule.

scenes.tts: Now predict what makes this curve bend. Must the food and shelter vanish completely? Or can crowding strengthen limits before they are gone? Keep your answer while the creek continues moving.
scenes.caption: Now predict what makes this curve bend. Must the food and shelter vanish completely? Or can crowding strengthen limits before they are gone? Keep your answer while the creek continues moving.
scenes.visual: Freeze only the rising graph marker. Keep water rippling, grass swaying and crabs walking. Place two large paths over the creek: 'resources gone' and 'limits strengthen sooner'. Do not highlight either path. End with the question still visible.
scenes.narration: Now predict what makes this curve bend. Must the food and shelter vanish completely? Or can crowding strengthen limits before they are gone? Keep your answer while the creek continues moving.

scenes.visual: Deliberate thinking pause. Keep both answer paths neutral. Continue slow water, grass and crab motion; pulse the question once near the end.

scenes.tts: Crowding means more crabs share the same food and shelter. Competition grows. Disease may spread more easily, and predators may find more prey. Fewer young survive for each crab already present. The population can still grow, but its growth slows before every resource disappears.
scenes.caption: Crowding means more crabs share the same food and shelter. Competition grows. Disease may spread more easily, and predators may find more prey. Fewer young survive for each crab already present. The population can still grow, but its growth slows before every resource disappears.
scenes.visual: Clear the choices. Move existing crabs closer around unchanged gold food and green shelter. Animate two crabs reaching the same food, then a red disease pulse passing between neighbours. Sweep a predator arrow across more nearby prey. Slow the population tracker's rise while some food and shelter remain visibly present.
scenes.narration: Crowding means more crabs share the same food and shelter. Competition grows. Disease may spread more easily, and predators may find more prey. Fewer young survive for each crab already present. The population can still grow, but its growth slows before every resource disappears.

scenes.tts: In the simplest limited-growth model, that slowing turns the jay into an ess. The computed line approaches carrying capacity. Carrying capacity is the largest population this environment can support over time, with its resources and challenges. It is a level approached, not a wall that nothing crosses.
scenes.caption: In the simplest limited-growth model, that slowing turns the J into an S. The computed line approaches carrying capacity. Carrying capacity is the largest population this environment can support over time, with its resources and challenges. It is a level approached, not a wall that nothing crosses.
scenes.visual: Transform the computed J curve into a computed logistic S curve using the same axes and starting point. Draw a gold dashed carrying-capacity guide. Let the teal curve approach the guide without drawing it as a wall. Keep 'computed model' visible.
scenes.narration: In the simplest limited-growth model, that slowing turns the J into an S. The computed line approaches carrying capacity. Carrying capacity is the largest population this environment can support over time, with its resources and challenges. It is a level approached, not a wall that nothing crosses.

scenes.tts: Read the ess-shaped curve from beginning to end. Growth starts slowly because few individuals can reproduce. Then numbers rise faster while resources are plentiful. Finally, growth slows near carrying capacity. With little movement in or out, births and deaths are about equal there.
scenes.caption: Read the S-shaped curve from beginning to end. Growth starts slowly because few individuals can reproduce. Then numbers rise faster while resources are plentiful. Finally, growth slows near carrying capacity. With little movement in or out, births and deaths are about equal there.
scenes.visual: Move one bright tracker along the same S curve. At the early segment, show a small teal group. At the steep segment, expand it. Near the guide, alternate a birth icon and death icon at equal displayed rates. Show the labels 'initial', 'faster' and 'slowing' only as the tracker reaches each region.
scenes.narration: Read the S-shaped curve from beginning to end. Growth starts slowly because few individuals can reproduce. Then numbers rise faster while resources are plentiful. Finally, growth slows near carrying capacity. With little movement in or out, births and deaths are about equal there.

scenes.tts: The computed line simply approaches carrying capacity. In real populations, births, deaths and movement continue. When that balance shifts, size can move up and down around the level. That balance, kept by ongoing change, is dynamic equilibrium. Real populations may also overshoot or decline. The ess shape is a useful model, not a required life story.

scenes.visual: Keep the computed teal S curve smooth as it approaches the gold guide; do not add any wobble to it. Beside it, draw a separate faint line labelled 'real population, schematic' that moves up and down around the guide while birth and death icons alternate. Then ghost three possible schematic continuations: overshoot, decline and a gentle wobble. Label each continuation 'schematic' and keep them faint so none looks inevitable. Return focus to the original S curve.

scenes.tts: Return to the creek. More crabs made the same resources harder to share, and several challenges grew stronger. Those limits reduced growth before the creek was empty. That is why the curve bent. The next question is whether the support level itself can move.

scenes.visual: Collapse the graph back into the creek. Replay the causal chain as one transformation: teal crabs crowd, sharing arrows divide the gold food and green shelter, red challenges strengthen, and the growth tracker slows. Remove every label except the gold capacity guide and the moving population tracker.

scenes.visual: Show one line only, centered and large: 'Limits slow population growth near carrying capacity.' No title, subtitle, logo or smaller line. Let a thin teal curve bend gently beneath the words without adding text.
